Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters Alaska Zuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boat Small cruise ship rescued skiff in south-east Alaska even though Meta billionaire’s $300m megayacht was closer Eric Berger Sun 9 Aug 2026 15.06 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 20.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Mark Zuckerberg has faced questions over why a small cruise ship in south-east Alaska rescued a stranded skiff and its crew when his 387ft superyacht had been closer. The Silicon Valley billionaire’s yacht, worth a reported $300m, is said to have “repeatedly” declined to assist when a nearby boat called for help last week. Zuckerberg, CEO of Facebook and Instagram owner Meta Platforms, was not on board at the time, a spokesperson told Forbes . When a nearby 21ft skiff ran out of fuel between Petersburg and Juneau, the Alaska Beacon reported operators of a cruise ship that was further away than Zuckerberg’s yacht came to the rescue. “I’m on a small-ship Alaska cruise with my son,” a passenger on the UnCruise Adventures ship Wilderness Legacy posted on Bluesky . “Our boat rescued a stranded vessel last night and apparently we did that after the Coast Guard radioed Mark Zuckerberg’s yacht – which was closer – and they repeatedly refused to respond. (There was near unanimous booing when the captain announced this).” But Brian Baker, a spokesperson for Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, told Forbes that the couple were not on board his yacht, named Launchpad. The yacht crew had been operating on a different radio channel, Baker told Forbes. “The assist was already under way” by the time they reviewed the broadcast, he said. Even if he was not on his ship, the report is unlikely to boost public opinion of Zuckerberg, who has faced criticism over the societal impact of his social media platforms; his new warm relationship with Donald Trump; and his lavish , insular lifestyle . “I live in Juneau and I’ve been having to look at that excessive eyesore parked up in [Auke Bay] for too long now,” a Reddit user wrote of the yacht in response to the rescue story. “Fuck Zuckerberg.” Explore more on these topics Alaska Mark Zuckerberg Meta news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/25/one-m.text: One million children in Afghanistan are suffering from life-threatening malnutrition in a worsening new crisis hitting the country, the United Nations warned on Tuesday.Across Afghanistan, 3.7 million children suffer from wasting, meaning they are acutely malnourished, the UN children's agency UNICEF said.Among that number are "one million children who are suffering from life-threatening severe acute malnutrition," UNICEF's Afghanistan country representative Tajudeen Oyewale said."If there is no treatment and we are not able to act fast, that one million number are at risk of dying," he told a media briefing in Geneva from Kabul.Afghanistan has endured repeated periods of widespread hunger in recent decades as it has struggled through civil war and other crises.An economic collapse followed the Taliban government's return to power after US-led forces withdrew in 2021.He said that nearly 40% of children admitted to hospitals with severe wasting and medical complications were babies under the age of six months old.Meanwhile children under two years old make up more than 80% of severe acute malnutrition cases in Afghanistan."Malnutrition plays a central role" in the growing numbers of deaths of very young children, Oyewale said.He described a "worsening nutrition crisis" across the country, with more than half a million children admitted to hospital so far this year for high risk, moderate and severe wasting.In July 2025, around 6,000 cases were recorded; in July this year, the numbers went above 8,000, a third higher."In parts of southern Afghanistan, some hospitals are now seeing three or four severe malnourished children for every available bed," he warned.

https://www.politico.eu/article/slovakia.text: BRUSSELS — The Slovak government on Wednesday rejected a 12-month extension for the EU's individual sanctions package against Russia, three diplomats told POLITICO. The measures — which have already been extended by six months many times before — expire on Sept. 15 . The bloc had hoped to secure a longer extension and avoid repeated renegotiations, but any amendment requires the unanimous support of all 27 member countries. The six-month renewal cycle was a compromise intended to placate former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Budapest used the recurring deadlines to press other EU governments for concessions. Advertisement Advertisement The bloc’s ambassadors could not find common ground on the proposal on Wednesday, with Slovakia being the sole holdout. “Apparently, they have some objections. I think we have heard them before,” one EU diplomat said. They were granted anonymity to comment freely on the closed-door negotiations. A spokesperson for the Slovak government declined to comment and shared a statement from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs: “Discussions on the regular six-month review of the sanctions regime … are ongoing and are expected to be concluded by 15 September 2026.” Talks also touched on adding a further 27 individuals and companies to the sanctions list, freezing their EU assets. Technical experts on sanctions policy will now discuss the changes and extension again. The law is one of the EU’s two main sanctions frameworks: individual and economic sanctions. Originally, both had to be renewed every six months, but the economic sanctions were extended for 12 months in June, after Orbán left office, and will now remain in force until July 2027. Nicholas Vinocur contributed to this report. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/05/us-m.text: Talks between US Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby and five European countries have raised concerns among NATO experts who warn the format risks dividing the alliance as Washington presses Europe to take greater responsibility for its own defence.Known as the Bergen Group after its inaugural meeting in Norway last year, the format brings together Sweden, Finland, Poland, Germany and the Netherlands.The UK, France and the Baltic states were not invited."The bottom line is this is very toxic for an alliance that relies of collective play," said Fabrice Pothier, CEO of geopolitical consultancy, Rasmussen Global."Clearly this is about the US having favourites," he told Euronews.The group was established to discuss NATO’s future as the alliance shifts towards so-called NATO 3.0: a US invented model in which Europe takes the lead the conventional defence of the continent.It also involves the US scaling back its traditional role, and withdrawing key capabilities including bombers, submarines and personnel it makes available to the alliance.Meanwhile, NATO is playing down the significance of the separate, US-led subgroup.“It’s not unusual for groups of Allies to meet in smaller formats,” a NATO official told Euronews.NATO 3.0 involves the US withdrawing from its traditional role as the leading defence provider in Europe, pulling capabilities such as bombers, submarines and personnel available to the alliance.While officials dismiss the talks as routine, others argue the arrangement will split members into "good European versus bad European" categories while reinforcing Washington's influence across the alliance. Pothier acknowledged that smaller groups can advance new ideas within organisations, such as the publication of 'non-papers', but he argued that Washington had selected the Bergen countries as they fulfil important defence criteria."Initiatives, often come from smaller groups," he said."These countries bring a certain desired mass – ground, air and maritime," said Pothier."But why is the US picking some rather than others when this is not a policy exercise?" he said.Pothier, who is former director of policy planning said the separation of the parts of alliance into subgroups creates concern that the US might be more inclined to defend one ally over another."You introduce the notion that the US favours some allies and would be likely to defend those allies ahead of the rest," said Pothier.He suggested US President Donald Trump’s “grudge” over the UK and France’s initial refusal to join the war in Iran, along with France’s push to buy European military equipment, could explain their exclusion.UK diplomats, however, rejected the suggestion that Britain was being sidelined, saying they remained in regular contact with their US counterparts.Baltic exclusion The Baltic states’ absence is particularly striking. They are among NATO’s biggest defence spenders as a share of GDP and sit on the alliance’s frontline with Russia. The region has faced repeated hybrid attacks, including drone incursions, arson and sabotage.Their exclusion follows Colby’s visit to NATO headquarters in Brussels in August, when, according to NATO sources, he urged Baltic officials to adopt a less confrontational tone towards Russian aggression.One source said Colby cited renewed US efforts to end the war in Ukraine as a reason to tone down talk of being at “war” with Russia.Washington has also invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami in December, at a golf resort owned by Trump."It's probably the first time since NATO enlargement that there’s a split between the US and Baltics," said Pothier."We know that this US administration is far less fazed by Russian aggression," he said.The situation for the Baltics remains tense due to the ongoing drone and other shadow war hostilities. Government, military and civilian populations are on constant alert. On Saturday, Vilnius airport was forced to shut down for around an hour, prompting the deployment of two NATO jets in response to a suspected drone intrusion from Belarus. Lithuania invites ColbyA source confirmed to Euronews that the Lithuanian government has invited Colby to visit the region to witness the ongoing airspace violations first-hand. "We say what we see," a Baltic diplomat told Euronews defending their forward military posture. The diplomat added that Moscow must understand the cost of its shadow war to be "harsh."EU Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius, a former Lithuanian prime minister, also called for a stronger response at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit last week."If we are hit by Russian hybrid attacks, our answers should be as painful as that attack," Kubilius said. Meanwhile, a Washington-based source told Euronews that the exclusive meeting appears to be "mischief-making" on the part of the US, warning that it actively divides the alliance. French officials had no response time of publication.

Europe Home page Europe 0 0 Sweden to deploy Patriot air defense system to Poland to protect Ukraine aid hub 06 October 2026 18:39 (UTC +04:00) Sweden will deploy a Patriot air defense system and around 100 military personnel to Poland to protect a NATO logistics hub supporting Ukraine, the Swedish Armed Forces said on Tuesday, Anadolu Agency reports. The deployment will safeguard the hub in Rzeszow against drones and missiles, taking over a mission currently carried out by the Netherlands. “This is the most complex operation that Sweden has undertaken as a NATO ally,” said Sofia Westermark, commander of Sweden’s Air Defense Regiment. The government-approved operation is scheduled to begin Dec. 1 and could last up to seven months, depending on decisions by the next government, according to public broadcaster SVT. “There is a threat to this location both from the ground and from the air, and as a NATO ally, we are participating with an air defense system to protect against drones and missiles,” Westermark said. According to SVT, authorities assess that Russia could seek to disrupt operations at the hub, which handles approximately 18,000 tons of equipment each month. “This location is extremely important, there are approximately 18,000 tons of equipment that flow through this logistics hub every month and for Ukraine it is important, and therefore it is important for us in NATO,” Westermark said. Asked how the deployment would affect Sweden’s domestic air defenses, she acknowledged that some military equipment would be stationed abroad. “Of course, it affects that part of our force is materially in another location, but we are NATO and right now we defend NATO best by solving this mission in Poland,” she said.
